title: Combinatorics and blockers
summary: How many combos a hand has on a board, and how your cards remove them.

count.text:
How many combos a hand has when some cards are already seen:
- **A pair**: with n cards of that rank left, n × (n − 1) / 2. All four left: 6 combos; one on the board: 3.
- **Two different cards**: n₁ × n₂. AK with no aces or kings seen: 4 × 4 = 16; with one ace on the board: 3 × 4 = 12.

labels: Sets on this flop: KK, 88 and 33, 3 combos each, 9 in all

blockers.text:
**Blockers** are cards you hold, so your opponent can't. Holding an ace means fewer aces for them:
- AA: 6 combos become **3**.
- AK: 16 combos become **12**.

Blockers help you choose bluffs: with the ace of the suit on a three-flush board, your opponent can't hold the nut flush and folds more often.

use.text: Combinatorics tells you what your opponent holds more often. Example: on K-8-3 they bet big. They have 9 set combos, but 12 of AK and 12 of KQ (if you don't hold a king). So "they bet because they have a set" is less likely than it feels.

q-aa.q: You hold As Kd. How many combos of AA can your opponent have?

t1.q: How many combos of AK are there with one ace on the board and no kings seen?

t2.q: How many combos of a set of eights are there on a K-8-3 flop?
t2.explain: One eight is on the board and three are left: 3 × 2 / 2 = 3.

t3.q: Why is the ace of the suit a good blocker for a bluff on a three-flush board?
options: Your opponent can't hold the nut flush
t3.explain: With the ace in your hand they can't have the best flush, so they fold more often.
